column14: What is important to you? Tell us about a problem you see in the world (big or small), what actions you’ve taken to make a positive impact, and what you learned.
column15: Community is a core pillar of CTC. Tell us about a community you felt like you truly belonged to. What aspects do you hope to bring into the CTC family?
column16: Write a short thank-you note acknowledging someone who has taught you something valuable and why it mattered (not a family member).
column17: Please briefly describe any relevant technical or group work experiences—it does not need to be extensive! For example, personal projects, internships, classes, or any technologies or projects that you’re excited about and would like to learn more about, etc.
column18: At CTC, one of our favorite traditions is Lightning Talks, where a member gives a short presentation on an interest, passion, or hobby of theirs—some topics from last year were how to DJ, a self defense workshop, and all about Niki Zefanya. What would you give a lightning talk on and why?
column19: Please list out any relevant classes you have taken so far or are taking at USC. Also, list out any planned commitments for the current school year and their estimated weekly time commitment.

column14: Unclaimed produce at the farmers market is small compared to what people usually write about here, which is exactly why nobody had fixed it. It is the kind of problem that never becomes urgent enough to fix, so it just quietly costs people hours every week forever. I started a weekly pickup that routes leftovers to a shelter downtown. I learned that a solution nobody adopts is worth less than no solution at all.
column15: The community I belonged to was a debate circuit that travelled by van, and it took me a year to notice it had become one. There was no hierarchy to speak of, which sounds idealistic and was mostly just practical: whoever knew how to do the thing did the thing, and taught the next person. The rule was that whoever knew the least got to ask first. What I would bring into CTC is that habit of making the entry cost low.
column16:
Dear Professor Diallo,

Thank you for teaching me that "good enough, shipped" beats "perfect, someday". You told me once, fairly bluntly, that I was hiding behind how much I had read. It was the most useful unkind thing anyone has said to me. I did not understand why it mattered until much later, when I caught myself doing it without deciding to.

— Yara
column17: I built a scheduling tool for the volunteer tutoring programme I coordinate. Swift for the app, and a Raspberry Pi doing something it was not designed for. I learned that the optimal schedule was the one everybody hated, because I had optimised for the wrong thing. I want to learn how to scope a project so it can ship in a semester.
column18: I would talk about the surprisingly bitter world of competitive crossword construction. I have given a version of this at a dinner table and it worked.
column19: CSCI 356, PSYC 314, CSCI 360, CSCI 201, CSCI 103; tutoring ~4 hrs/week

column14: The problem I picked is e-waste from campus upgrades, which sounds minor until you count how many hours it costs the people carrying it. I spent last summer working somewhere it was impossible to ignore, and the pattern was always the same: the people closest to it had known about it for years and had never been asked. I built a spreadsheet, then an actual tool, that matches donations to need. It took about six weeks before anyone used it without being asked, and that was the real milestone rather than the day it worked. What I learned is that the most consequential decision in a project like this is usually not a technical one.
column15: The community that shaped me most was a 6am swim squad nobody else wanted to join, mostly because it was bad at hierarchy. The whole thing ran on Sunday evenings, which meant everyone there had chosen it over something easier. It ran on a hundred small favours nobody kept score of. What I would bring to CTC is the unglamorous maintenance that keeps a community alive: the reminder message, the booked room, the noticing that somebody has gone quiet.
column16:

The specific moment I keep returning to is the afternoon I handed in something I knew was mediocre, and instead of grading it you asked me what I would change if I had another week.
